---
title: "Authorship attribution"
---

Quarto can surface per-node authorship information in rendered output,
sourcing it from `git blame` on the command line or from the Automerge
edit history inside the hub-client. The feature is **opt-in**: nothing
is emitted unless you ask for it.

## Privacy and discoverability

Attribution writes author email addresses (or display names supplied
by the producer) into the rendered HTML. **Anyone with access to the
output can read them** — and they survive as `data-attr-*` attributes
even on static hosts, including those served by GitHub Pages, Netlify,
or behind a CDN. Treat the rendered output as having the same
exposure surface as a public commit log.

If that's not the right tradeoff for a given project, leave attribution
off. The CLI and YAML defaults are both off; there is no implicit
enablement.

## Enabling attribution on the command line

Pass `--attribution=git` when invoking `quarto render`:

```bash
quarto render report.qmd --attribution=git
```

Quarto shells out to `git blame --porcelain` for the input file,
maps each line to an author email and commit timestamp, and emits the
result on every wrapped node in the rendered HTML.

To turn attribution off explicitly — for example when overriding a
YAML default — use `--attribution=off`.

## Enabling attribution via YAML

The same setting is available in document YAML:

```yaml
---
title: My report
attribution: git
---
```

The two values supported in v1 are `git` (run the `git blame`
provider) and `off` (no attribution, identical to the default).

### CLI overrides YAML

When the CLI flag and document YAML disagree, the CLI wins. This
makes `--attribution=off` a reliable escape hatch even on documents
that opt in by default:

| `--attribution` | YAML `attribution` | Effective mode |
|---|---|---|
| (unset)         | (unset)            | off            |
| (unset)         | `off`              | off            |
| (unset)         | `git`              | git            |
| `off`           | (unset)            | off            |
| `off`           | `git`              | **off** (CLI wins) |
| `git`           | (unset)            | git            |
| `git`           | `off`              | **git** (CLI wins) |
| `git`           | `git`              | git            |

### Supplying custom display names

The `git` provider derives a display name and colour from each
author's email automatically. The display name is the mail-local-part
of the address; the colour is a deterministic entry from Paul Tol's
[Muted qualitative palette](https://sronpersonalpages.nl/~pault/) —
a 10-colour, colour-blind-safe scheme designed for categorical
encoding. If you want different labels — for instance to spell out
"Alice Cooper" instead of `alice` — override them in YAML:

```yaml
---
title: My report
attribution:
  source: git
  identities:
    alice@example.com:
      display_name: "Alice Cooper"
      color: "#c0392b"
    bob@example.com:
      display_name: "Bob Roberts"
---
```

User identity entries are merged on top of provider-supplied ones:
a key present in both takes the YAML value. Keys present **only** in
YAML are dropped — overrides are matched against actors the provider
actually reports, so a stale entry can't silently inject a phantom
author.

## What attribution looks like in the output

Each wrapping element carries two data attributes that identify the
author and edit time for that node:

```html
<span data-attr-actor="alice@example.com" data-attr-time="1700000000">
  …
</span>
```

- `data-attr-actor` — the raw actor identifier (the author email for
  `git`, an Automerge actor ID inside the hub).
- `data-attr-time` — Unix epoch timestamp of the most recent commit
  (or edit) touching the wrapped range. The `git` provider emits
  **seconds**; the hub-client (Automerge) emits **milliseconds**.
  Consumers that handle both should use a threshold like `< 1e12` to
  tell them apart.

The author's display name and colour are emitted **once per author**
as a CSS rule in the rendered `<head>`, exposing two custom
properties that any element matching the actor inherits via the
cascade:

```html
<style>
  [data-attr-actor="alice@example.com"] {
      --attr-color: #117733;
      --attr-name: "alice";
  }
  …
</style>
```

`--attr-color` is consumed by the default viewer's base paint rule
(see [Default viewer](#viewer-overlay)) so authored prose appears in
the author's colour without any further wiring. `--attr-name`
is read by the hover badge from each wrapper's computed style.
Consuming themes can override either via a higher-specificity rule
in their own stylesheet without touching the rendered HTML.

Contiguous prose authored by the same actor at the same time
coalesces into a single outer wrapper, so a paragraph written by one
person produces one wrapper rather than one per word. Structured
inlines (links, code, math, etc.) always get their own wrapper.

## Default viewer {#viewer-overlay}

By default, `--attribution=git` (or YAML `attribution: git`) ships a
small inline `<style>` and `<script>` pair alongside the wrappers, so
the rendered HTML is visibly attributed out of the box: attributed
prose appears in the author's colour with a dotted underline, and
hovering surfaces a small author-coloured badge with the contributor's
name and a relative timestamp.

The per-author colour comes from the `--attr-color` CSS custom
property published by the per-actor rule in `<head>` (see [What
attribution looks like in the output](#what-attribution-looks-like-in-the-output));
the inherited paint rule lives in the auto-injected viewer
stylesheet, and the hover badge reads `--attr-name` from the same
source. To recolour an author site-wide, override the custom property
in your own stylesheet with a higher-specificity rule — no HTML
changes required.

### Turning the default viewer off

If you want only the `data-attr-*` attributes (e.g. you have a site
theme that styles them differently, or you are wiring up a custom
overlay), suppress the default viewer with the rich-form YAML:

```yaml
---
title: My report
attribution:
  source: git
  viewer: false
---
```

The per-node `data-attr-actor` / `data-attr-time` wrappers remain
exactly as before; only the auto-injected CSS rules (including the
per-actor `--attr-color` / `--attr-name` declarations) and the hover
`<script>` are dropped. A theme that wants to render its own colours
should publish its own per-actor rules in the same shape:

```css
[data-attr-actor="alice@example.com"] {
    --attr-color: #c0392b;
    --attr-name: "Alice Cooper";
}
```

### Customizing presentation

Whether or not the default viewer is on, the per-node
`data-attr-actor` / `data-attr-time` attrs are the stable contract.
A site theme can key off `data-attr-actor` to colour authored
regions however it likes, and a custom Pandoc filter can transform
the wrappers without touching this package.

## Hub-client integration

The Quarto hub client ships the same attribution data path,
sourcing actors from the Automerge edit history of the live document
rather than from `git blame`. The data wire is in place; the
in-product toggle and renderer-side colouring are still in
development — when they land, an "Authorship" control will appear in
the document settings.

## Using attribution in Lua filters

When a provider is installed (`--attribution=git` on the CLI, or the
hub-client preview path), user Lua filters can query the same
attribution sidecar through the `quarto.attribution.*` host binding.
Both pre-phase (`pre-quarto`) and post-phase filters see it.

### Example: colour spans by author

```lua
function Span(elem)
    local hit = quarto.attribution.lookup(elem)
    if hit then
        local attr = pandoc.Attr(
            elem.attr.identifier,
            elem.attr.classes,
            { ["data-author"] = hit.name, ["style"] = "color: " .. hit.color }
        )
        return pandoc.Span(elem.content, attr)
    end
    return elem
end
```

`quarto.attribution.lookup(el)` returns either `nil` or a table:

```lua
{
    actor = "alice@example.com",  -- the producer's actor id (email for git)
    time  = 1715000000000,        -- Unix epoch milliseconds
    name  = "Alice",              -- resolved display name
    color = "#ff0000",            -- resolved CSS-compatible colour
}
```

It returns `nil` when:

- the element has no source-file provenance (synthesised nodes,
  `RawInline`/`RawBlock` injected by upstream filters);
- the resolved file ID is non-primary (v1 is single-document — a node
  spliced in via `{{< include other.qmd >}}` returns `nil`);
- no run in the sidecar overlaps the element's byte range;
- no provider is installed (i.e. attribution is off).

### Primitive: arbitrary byte ranges

When you have explicit `(start, end)` offsets — say from a custom
text-walking transform — bypass element lookup with the raw form:

```lua
local raw = quarto.attribution.lookup_range(0, 100)
-- => { actor = "alice@example.com", time = 1715000000000 }
--    (no `name`/`color` — identity is *not* joined for the raw call)
```

Use `quarto.attribution.identities()` to look identities up
separately:

```lua
local idents = quarto.attribution.identities()
local alice = idents["alice@example.com"]
-- alice = { name = "Alice", color = "#ff0000" }
```

The identity map is read-only and empty when no provider is
installed.

### Read-only contract

The Lua binding is v1 read-only. There is no
`quarto.attribution.set(el, actor, time)` — filters can transform the
AST freely, but the underlying attribution sidecar is derived from
the source (`git blame` for the CLI; Automerge edit history for the
hub-client preview) and is not user-mutable. Bake whatever
presentation you want from the read side instead.

## Current limits

- **Single-document blame only.** Content spliced in via
  `{{< include other.qmd >}}` is not attributed in v1; the wrappers
  for included nodes will be absent. A future release will extend
  blame across the entire include chain.
- **No caching.** Each render re-runs `git blame`. On a 100 K-line
  file this completes in roughly 50 ms, so caching is not currently a
  bottleneck.
- **No project-wide aggregation.** Each document's attribution is
  scoped to that document; cross-document summaries ("Alice
  contributed to N pages") are a future feature.
